name: NAIC on Artificial Intelligence in Insurance: Topic Overview, Working Group and Health AI/ML Survey
title: NAIC on Artificial Intelligence in Insurance: Topic Overview, Working Group and Health AI/ML Survey
answer: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners publishes a topic overview, a working group page and a health data call on AI in insurance. The most useful item is the survey evidence: of responding carriers, 88% of auto insurers, 70% of home insurers, 58% of life companies and 92% of health insurers said they use, plan to use or plan to explore AI or machine learning models.

sections.body: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the body coordinating US state insurance regulators, publishes these pages on content.naic.org. Three were read: an insurance topic overview explaining artificial intelligence and how it is used and regulated in the industry, the committee page for the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group, and the data call page for the Health AI/ML Survey dated November 11, 2024. Together they set out the NAIC's regulatory activity on AI rather than a single dated report.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The overview defines AI as technology letting computer systems perform tasks that usually require human intelligence, including analysing data, images, video and sound, summarising information and generating content. In insurance it is used in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing and fraud detection. Chatbots answer common questions and assist with simple transactions at any time of day, and claims processing uses AI to estimate repair costs or assess damage from photos and historical data. AI may move insurers from detect and repair toward predict and prevent. Large language models such as CoPilot, ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can answer questions and summarise documents but may generate information that sounds accurate yet is incorrect. The text expects AI to support rather than replace actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents and customer service representatives. Insurers remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, standards and consumer protection rules, including fairness, accuracy and avoiding unfair discrimination, and state regulators may require companies to explain how tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing or claims decisions. The Working Group researches big data and AI, monitors state, federal and international activity, supports adoption of the Model Bulletin on the Use of AI Systems by Insurers, and develops evaluation tools and training for regulators.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The overview reports that of 193 auto insurers responding, 88% use, plan to use or plan to explore AI or machine learning models; of 194 home insurers, 70%; of 161 life companies, 58%; and of 93 health insurers, 92%. The Working Group was established in 2019, the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee in 2021, and regulatory principles on AI were adopted at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Survey reports appeared in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023 and May 2025. The health survey covers 16 participating states and applies to health insurers with more than $250 million of earned health insurance premium in 2023.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: This is the regulatory layer US carriers answer to on underwriting AI. The overview states the expectations on fairness, accuracy and discrimination, and confirms that regulators may ask how tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing or claims. The working group page shows where the rules are heading, including the Model Bulletin and an AI Systems Evaluation Tool being tested. The survey figures give a reader a rare line-of-business view of adoption, showing health and auto far ahead of life.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Insurance

sections.body: The pages are regulator-facing and describe process and expectations rather than prescribing detailed technical standards. The adoption figures are self-reported survey responses, not audited counts, and the health survey is limited to companies writing in the 16 participating states, though responses are national in scope. The overview is explanatory and undated, and the working group page reports activity without full minutes.
